Aim and objectives

Aim. To calculate and interpret the measures of diagnostic test performance from a 2×2 table.

At the end of this workbook, you should be able to:

  1. Calculate sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV from a diagnostic 2×2 table.
  2. Explain why predictive values change with prevalence while sensitivity and specificity do not.
  3. Calculate positive and negative likelihood ratios and use a Fagan nomogram to find post-test probability.
  4. Interpret a ROC curve and explain what an area under the curve of 0.5 and 1.0 mean.

Part 1 · Core ideas

Category 113.2 · Diagnostic accuracy

3.2.5Sensitivity, specificity and likelihood ratios

Big idea. Sensitivity and specificity describe the test and never change; what changes from clinic to clinic is what a result means for the patient in front of you.
Picture it as a smoke alarm in a kitchen.

Syllabus: Sensitivity, specificity, false positive and false negative rates, likelihood ratios

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 79 · Sensitivity and specificity →

The story in plain words. Think of a smoke alarm. A sensitive alarm goes off for almost every real fire, which is what you want from a device meant to miss nothing. Sensitivity is a / (a + c): of everyone who truly has the disease, the share the test picks up. You read it down the disease-present column. A specific alarm stays quiet for burnt toast. Specificity is d / (b + d): of everyone truly free of the disease, the share the test correctly clears. That is the disease-absent column. Both are properties of the alarm itself, and neither changes when you move the alarm to a different kitchen. ((? If a hospital's prevalence doubles, what happens to sensitivity? ?)) Nothing at all. It is a property of the test, not of the population. The two trade off against each other. Lower the cut-off and the alarm becomes twitchier: sensitivity rises, specificity falls. Raise it and the reverse happens. The false positive rate is 1 minus specificity, the false negative rate is 1 minus sensitivity.

Sensitivity reads down a column. Predictive value reads across a row.
Disease presentDisease absentRow total
Test positivea
true positive		b
false positive		a + b
PPV = a/(a+b)
Test negativec
false negative		d
true negative		c + d
NPV = d/(c+d)
Column totala + c
Sens = a/(a+c)		b + d
Spec = d/(b+d)		n

Down the columns: properties of the test, fixed whatever the population. Across the rows: what the result means for this patient, and therefore dependent on prevalence.

The people and the evidence. Altman and Bland (1994) set out the pair in the BMJ series the exam is built on, and Sackett's Clinical Epidemiology gave us the two mnemonics that survive every revision course. SnNout: a Sensitive test, when Negative, rules out. SpPin: a Specific test, when Positive, rules in. Deeks and Altman (2004) made the case for likelihood ratios instead. LR+ is sensitivity divided by 1 minus specificity: how much more likely this positive result is in disease than in health. LR- is 1 minus sensitivity, divided by specificity. An LR of 1 is a test that told you nothing.

From everyday life to the clinic. Likelihood ratios are the useful form at the bedside because they combine with what you already believed. Post-test odds equal pre-test odds times the likelihood ratio, and because the ratio is a property of the test it transfers between populations unchanged. The rules of thumb are worth holding. An LR+ above 10 or an LR- below 0.1 shifts a diagnosis decisively. Between 5 and 10, or 0.1 and 0.2, the shift is moderate. Near 1, the test has wasted everyone's morning.

A smoke alarm: sensitivity is how many real fires it catches (9 of 10 = 90%); specificity is how many quiet kitchens it leaves in peace (81 of 90 = 90%)

Where the exam tries to catch you. The commonest error is reading the table the wrong way. Sensitivity and specificity run down the columns; anything read across a row is a predictive value and behaves quite differently. The second is forgetting that a cut-off is a choice, not a fact. A question that changes the threshold is asking you to move sensitivity and specificity in opposite directions. The third is treating SnNout and SpPin as interchangeable: the sensitive test is for ruling out, and only when it is negative.

Sources
  1. Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 2: predictive values. BMJ, 309: 102.
  2. Hanley JA, McNeil BJ (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143: 29-36.
  3. Fagan TJ (1975). Nomogram for Bayes theorem. NEJM, 293: 257.

3.2.6Predictive values and prevalence

Big idea. The same test, unchanged, gives a different answer to the patient depending on how common the disease is where you are standing.
Picture it as the same alarm in a kitchen and in a fireworks factory.

Syllabus: Positive and negative predictive values, and the effect of prevalence

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 86 · Predictive values and prevalence →

The story in plain words. Move the smoke alarm into a fireworks factory and nothing about the device changes, yet when it sounds you believe it. That belief is the positive predictive value: a / (a + b), the share of test positives who truly have the disease. Its partner, the negative predictive value, is d / (c + d). Predictive values are read across the rows, and they answer the question the patient actually asked. Sensitivity and specificity answer the laboratory's question. Prevalence, which is (a + c) divided by the total, is the pre-test probability in that population, and it is what decides which way the rows fall. As prevalence rises, PPV rises and NPV falls. As it falls, the reverse. ((? Which four figures stay fixed while all this happens? ?)) Sensitivity, specificity and both likelihood ratios. They belong to the test.

The same test, two populations. Only the prevalence changed.
SettingPrevalenceSensitivitySpecificityPPVNPV
Open-access clinic25%80%80%57%92%
Specialist ward60%80%80%86%73%

Sensitivity and specificity did not move. The answer to the patient's question moved a great deal.

The people and the evidence. Altman and Bland (1994) worked the arithmetic that makes the point unarguable. Take 400 attenders at an open-access clinic with a prevalence of 25%, and a test that is 80% sensitive and 80% specific. You get 80 true positives and 60 false positives, so the PPV is 57%: a positive result is barely better than a coin. Run the identical test on a specialist ward where prevalence is 60% and the PPV climbs to 86% while the NPV drops from 92% to 73%. Nothing was done to the test.

From everyday life to the clinic. This is the whole argument against screening a low-risk population for a rare disorder. Even an excellent test generates mostly false positives when the condition is uncommon, and every false positive is a real person given a frightening letter and an unnecessary investigation. It is also why a result must always be read against the setting. The same questionnaire score means one thing in a community sample and quite another in a tertiary referral clinic, and a clinician who does not adjust for that will over-diagnose on the ward and under-diagnose in the community.

The same alarm (90% sensitive, 90% specific) in two buildings: when it rings in the restaurant it is usually right (27 of 34); in the office most rings are false alarms (2 of 12). That is prevalence changing the predictive value

Where the exam tries to catch you. The classic stem gives you a good test, a rare disease and asks why most positives are wrong. The answer is low prevalence, not a poor test. The second trap offers you sensitivity when the question asked for PPV: check whether the denominator is everyone with the disease or everyone with a positive result. The third is the assumption that a high NPV is reassurance. In a low-prevalence setting the NPV is high no matter how bad the test is, simply because almost nobody has the disease.

Sources
  1. Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.
  2. Hanley JA, McNeil BJ (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology, 143: 29-36.

3.2.7Nomograms and ROC curves

Big idea. A test does not give you a diagnosis, it moves you from what you believed before to what you should believe now, and both the nomogram and the ROC curve exist to show that movement.
Picture it as a ruler laid across three scales.

Syllabus: Fagan nomogram, pre-test and post-test probability, receiver operating characteristic curves

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 96 · ROC curves, AUC and cut-off →

The story in plain words. The arithmetic of a test result is three steps. Turn your pre-test probability into odds, p divided by 1 minus p. Multiply by the likelihood ratio of the result you got. Turn it back, odds divided by 1 plus odds. A 20% pre-test probability with an LR+ of 6 gives odds of 0.25 times 6, which is 1.5, which is a post-test probability of 60%. The Fagan nomogram does that arithmetic with a ruler. Three vertical scales: pre-test probability on the left, likelihood ratio in the middle, post-test probability on the right. Lay the ruler from your pre-test probability through the likelihood ratio and read where it crosses the right-hand scale. Use LR+ for a positive result and LR- for a negative one. The ROC curve asks a different question: not what this result means, but how good the test is at every possible cut-off. Plot sensitivity on the vertical against 1 minus specificity on the horizontal, once for each threshold, and join the points.

The ROC curve plots every possible cut-off at once: moving along the curve trades specificity for sensitivity, and the area under it is the chance that a random case scores higher than a random non-case

The people and the evidence. Fagan (1975) published his nomogram in a single-page letter to the New England Journal of Medicine, and it has outlived almost everything published alongside it, because likelihood ratios transfer between populations and so the nomogram works anywhere. Altman and Bland (1994) set out the ROC curve in the same BMJ series. The diagonal is a test that does nothing, with an area under the curve of 0.5. A perfect test reaches the top left corner, area 1.0.

From everyday life to the clinic. The area under the curve has a meaning worth memorising: it is the probability that a randomly chosen case scores higher than a randomly chosen non-case. Between 0.7 and 0.8 is acceptable, 0.8 to 0.9 good, above 0.9 excellent. Choosing a cut-off is a clinical decision, not a statistical one. The point nearest the top left corner balances the two errors equally, which is right only when the two errors cost the same. ((? Where would you move the cut-off for a test that triages suicide risk? ?)) Towards sensitivity, because missing a case costs far more than a false alarm.

The dial on the alarm is the cut-off: turn it down and you catch every fire but suffer false alarms; turn it up and you sleep through some fires. Every setting is one point on the ROC curve

Where the exam tries to catch you. The axes are the trap. It is sensitivity against 1 minus specificity, not against specificity, and drawing it the other way turns a good test into a bad one. The second is forgetting that the ROC curve, like its ingredients, is independent of prevalence: it compares tests, it does not tell you what a result means for a patient. The third is reading an area under the curve of 0.5 as a small effect rather than as no effect at all. It is the diagonal, and the diagonal is a coin.

Sources
  1. Fagan TJ (1975). Nomogram for Bayes's theorem. N Engl J Med, 293: 257.
  2. Fagan TJ (1975). Nomogram for Bayes theorem. NEJM, 293: 257.
  3. Deeks JJ, Altman DG (2004). Diagnostic tests 4: likelihood ratios. BMJ, 329: 168-169.

Screening questionnaire for anxiety disorder against a structured diagnostic interview in 1,000 antenatal clinic attenders
A seven-item anxiety questionnaire is given to 1,000 women attending an antenatal clinic, and every woman is also assessed with a structured diagnostic interview as the reference standard. The results are shown in the table. What is the sensitivity of the questionnaire?
  1. 0.33
  2. 0.80
  3. 0.90
  4. 0.99
  5. 4.5
Show the working
Answer: C 0.90

Sensitivity is the proportion of people who truly have the condition that the test correctly flags. It is calculated entirely within the diseased column of the 2x2 table and does not change with prevalence, which is why it is called a property of the test rather than of the population.

In the table the disorder-present column contains 90 true positives and 10 false negatives, 100 women in all. Sensitivity = 90/100 = 0.90: the questionnaire detects nine in ten cases and misses one in ten.

The exam puts PPV (0.33), specificity (0.80) and NPV (0.99) in the same option list. Decide first which column or row the question is asking about: sensitivity and specificity are columns (truth), predictive values are rows (test result).

Rule: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN): read down the 'disorder present' column.
Trap: Dividing true positives by all test positives (the PPV) instead of all true cases.
Sensitivity lives entirely in the disorder-present column: 90 of every 100 true cases are flagged, 10 are missed, sensitivity = 0.90

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308: 1552.

A seven-item anxiety questionnaire is given to 1,000 women attending an antenatal clinic, and every woman is also assessed with a structured diagnostic interview as the reference standard. The results are shown in the table. What is the specificity of the questionnaire?
  1. 0.20
  2. 0.33
  3. 0.80
  4. 0.90
  5. 0.99
Show the working
Answer: C 0.80

Specificity is the proportion of people who truly do not have the condition that the test correctly clears. Like sensitivity it is calculated within one column of the table, the non-diseased column, and it is independent of prevalence.

Here the disorder-absent column has 180 false positives and 720 true negatives, 900 women in total. Specificity = 720/900 = 0.80. One woman in five without an anxiety disorder still screens positive, which is the false positive rate of 0.20.

The exam tests whether you can keep the four quantities apart in one table. Specificity and NPV both involve true negatives, but specificity divides by the truth column (900) and NPV by the test-negative row (730).

Rule: Specificity = TN / (TN + FP): read down the 'disorder absent' column.
Trap: Dividing true negatives by all test negatives (the NPV) instead of all truly well people.
StepWorkingResult
False positivesQuestionnaire positive and disorder absent180
True negativesQuestionnaire negative and disorder absent720
Column total180 + 720900 women without the disorder
Specificity720 / 9000.80
Specificity uses only the disorder-absent column: 720 of the 900 women without an anxiety disorder are correctly cleared, so specificity = 0.80

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308: 1552.

Screening questionnaire for anxiety disorder against a structured diagnostic interview in 1,000 antenatal clinic attenders
A seven-item anxiety questionnaire is given to 1,000 women attending an antenatal clinic, and every woman is also assessed with a structured diagnostic interview as the reference standard. The results are shown in the table. What is the likelihood ratio for a positive questionnaire result?
  1. 0.125
  2. 0.72
  3. 1.125
  4. 4.5
  5. 9
Show the working
Answer: D 4.5

The positive likelihood ratio compares the probability of a positive result in someone with the condition (the sensitivity) with the probability of a positive result in someone without it (the false positive rate, 1 minus specificity). Because it uses only the two column-based proportions, it is independent of prevalence, and it multiplies pre-test odds into post-test odds.

From the table sensitivity is 0.90 and specificity is 0.80, so the false positive rate is 0.20. LR+ = 0.90/0.20 = 4.5. A positive screen is four and a half times as likely in a woman with an anxiety disorder as in one without. Applied to pre-test odds of 1:9 (prevalence 10%) it gives post-test odds of 4.5:9 = 0.5, a post-test probability of 0.33, which is exactly the PPV.

The exam offers sensitivity divided by specificity as the trap. Remember the denominator is the false positive rate; a test with specificity 0.80 'leaks' 20% false positives, and the LR is sensitivity divided by that leak.

Rule: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 minus specificity): how much more often a positive result occurs in cases than in non-cases.
Trap: Dividing sensitivity by specificity rather than by 1 minus specificity.
A positive result appears in 90 of 100 with the disorder and 20 of 100 without: LR+ = 90/20 = 4.5

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 2: predictive values. BMJ, 309: 102.

Challenge 6 · 13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.5
Nomogram for a depression screening questionnaire used in a diabetes clinic: pre-test probability 20%, positive likelihood ratio 8
A depression screening questionnaire is used in a diabetes outpatient clinic. Previous work has established that 20% of attenders at this clinic have a depressive disorder. The questionnaire has a sensitivity of 80% and a specificity of 90%. The nomogram is provided. What is the likelihood ratio for a positive questionnaire result?
  1. 0.22
  2. 0.9
  3. 4
  4. 8
  5. 10
Show the working
Answer: D 8

The positive likelihood ratio is the ratio of the probability of a positive result in people with the condition to the probability of a positive result in people without it. The numerator is the sensitivity; the denominator is the false positive rate, 1 minus specificity. It depends only on the test, not on prevalence.

Sensitivity is 0.80 and specificity 0.90, so the false positive rate is 0.10. LR+ = 0.80/0.10 = 8: a positive questionnaire is eight times as common in depressed attenders as in non-depressed ones. The negative likelihood ratio, for completeness, is 0.20/0.90 = 0.22.

The exam habitually offers LR minus and sensitivity over specificity as distractors. Write the formula, substitute, and check that an LR+ above 1 makes the condition more likely.

Rule: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 minus specificity); it is the middle axis of the nomogram.
Trap: Confusing LR+ with LR minus, or using specificity rather than 1 minus specificity in the denominator.
StepWorkingResult
SensitivityPositive results among the depressed0.80
False positive rate1 minus specificity = 1 minus 0.900.10
LR+0.80 / 0.108
LR minus, for contrast(1 minus 0.80) / 0.900.22
The positive likelihood ratio is sensitivity over the false positive rate, 0.80/0.10 = 8; the negative likelihood ratio of 0.22 is the tempting distractor

Source: Fagan TJ (1975). Nomogram for Bayes theorem. NEJM, 293: 257.

Four-item gambling screen (score 0 to 4) against a structured diagnostic interview in 500 attenders at a debt advice service
A four-item screening questionnaire for gambling disorder, scored from 0 to 4, is completed by 500 attenders at a debt advice service. Every attender is also assessed with a structured diagnostic interview as the reference standard. The table shows the number of attenders at each score with and without gambling disorder. A screen is positive when the score is at or above the chosen cut-off. What is the sensitivity of the questionnaire if the cut-off is a score of 2 or more?
  1. 0.20
  2. 0.50
  3. 0.80
  4. 0.89
  5. 0.96
Show the working
Answer: C 0.80

To find sensitivity at a given cut-off, first decide who counts as a screen positive (everyone scoring at or above the cut-off), then look only at the column of people who truly have the condition. Sensitivity is the number of true cases who are screen positive divided by all true cases.

At a cut-off of 2 or more, the screen positives among the 50 cases are those scoring 2 (15), 3 (15) and 4 (10): 40 in total. Sensitivity = 40/50 = 0.80. The 10 cases scoring 0 or 1 are the false negatives. For reference, specificity at this cut-off is (330 + 70)/450 = 0.89.

The exam's multi-row table is designed to make you add the wrong rows. Draw a line at the cut-off, sum everything on the positive side of it in the disease column, and divide by the column total.

Rule: Collapse the table at the cut-off: sensitivity = cases at or above the cut-off / all cases.
Trap: Counting only the row for the cut-off score (15/50) instead of that row and everything above it.
StepWorkingResult
Screen positives among casesScores 2, 3 and 4: 15 + 15 + 1040
All casesColumn total50
Sensitivity40 / 500.80
Specificity, for reference(330 + 70) / 4500.89
At a cut-off of 2 or more, 40 of the 50 attenders with gambling disorder screen positive, sensitivity 0.80; the 10 scoring 0 or 1 are the false negatives

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308: 1552.

Performance of five autism screening instruments against a multidisciplinary consensus diagnosis
The table shows the performance of five screening instruments for autism in children referred to a community paediatric service. The service has ample capacity for full diagnostic assessment and wants to be sure that children with autism are not missed at the screening stage. Which instrument should be chosen?
  1. Instrument A
  2. Instrument B
  3. Instrument C
  4. Instrument D
  5. Instrument E
Show the working
Answer: B Instrument B

Sensitivity is the proportion of true cases the test identifies; 1 minus sensitivity is the false negative rate. Specificity is the proportion of non-cases correctly cleared; 1 minus specificity is the false positive rate. A screening step that must not miss cases prioritises sensitivity and accepts false positives, provided the downstream service can assess them.

Instrument B at 94% sensitivity misses 6 in 100 children with autism; Instrument D at 51% misses 49. The price of Instrument B is a 48% false positive rate among unaffected children, which the stem tells you the service can handle.

If the stem had said diagnostic resources were scarce, the balance would shift towards specificity or a combined measure such as the likelihood ratio.

Rule: When missing a case is the worst outcome and follow-up capacity is good, choose the most sensitive test.
Trap: Choosing the instrument with the best overall balance rather than the one the stated priority demands.
When the brief is not to miss cases, Instrument B lets 6 of 100 affected children slip through while Instrument D misses 49

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308: 1552.

Challenge 9 · 13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.5
MethodSensitivitySpecificity
Bedside number connection test (Dr Okafor)85%94%
EEG index (Dr Lindqvist)92%94%
Sensitivity and specificity of the two methods for hepatic encephalopathy
Two clinicians disagree about the best way to detect hepatic encephalopathy on a liver unit. Dr Okafor uses a bedside number connection test with sensitivity 85% and specificity 94%. Dr Lindqvist uses a new electroencephalographic index with sensitivity 92% and specificity 94%. The table shows the two sets of figures. If 150 patients are assessed with both methods, which statement is correct?
  1. Dr Okafor will correctly identify more patients with encephalopathy than Dr Lindqvist
  2. Dr Okafor will correctly identify more patients without encephalopathy than Dr Lindqvist
  3. Dr Okafor will correctly identify fewer patients with encephalopathy than Dr Lindqvist
  4. Dr Okafor will make no false diagnoses
  5. The prevalence of encephalopathy must be known before the two can be compared
Show the working
Answer: C Dr Okafor will correctly identify fewer patients with encephalopathy than Dr Lindqvist

Sensitivity is the proportion of truly affected patients that a test picks up. When two tests have the same specificity, the only difference in how they perform is in the diseased column, and the more sensitive test will always identify more cases.

Here specificity is 94% for both, so each clinician wrongly labels the same 6% of unaffected patients. Among the affected, Dr Okafor's test detects 85 of every 100 and Dr Lindqvist's detects 92 of every 100. Whatever the prevalence, the ratio of true positives is fixed by sensitivity alone.

The exam tempts you with 'prevalence is needed'. Prevalence matters for predictive values and for the absolute numbers, but not for which test finds a larger share of the diseased.

Rule: Among the diseased, the test with the higher sensitivity finds more cases, at any prevalence.
Trap: Thinking prevalence must be known to compare the number of true positives detected.
Among the same 100 affected patients Dr Okafor's test finds 85 and misses 15 while Dr Lindqvist's finds 92 and misses 8; specificity, 94% for both, plays no part in this comparison.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308: 1552.

Challenge 10 · 13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.5

Results of a brief questionnaire and a urine assay in 400 attenders at a community drug service, against a structured diagnostic interview
A brief questionnaire and a urine assay were both applied to 400 attenders at a community drug service, of whom 250 were found on structured interview to have opioid dependence. The table shows the results. Compared with the questionnaire, the urine assay has
  1. Lower sensitivity and lower specificity
  2. Higher sensitivity and lower specificity
  3. The same sensitivity and specificity
  4. Lower sensitivity and higher specificity
  5. Higher sensitivity and higher specificity
Show the working
Answer: D Lower sensitivity and higher specificity

To compare two tests you work down the columns of the reference standard. The diseased column gives sensitivity (true positives over all with the disease); the non-diseased column gives specificity (true negatives over all without it). The row totals are never used for these two measures.

Questionnaire: 200 of 250 dependent people screened positive, sensitivity 80%; 120 of 150 non-dependent people screened negative, specificity 80%. Urine assay: 175 of 250 positive, sensitivity 70%; 135 of 150 negative, specificity 90%. So the assay misses more cases but mislabels fewer non-cases.

The exam will present the four lines in a different order or hide the column totals; always rebuild the two 2x2 tables before comparing.

Rule: Sensitivity = TP / all diseased; specificity = TN / all non-diseased, each read down its own column.
Trap: Reading the assay's 175 positives as higher sensitivity simply because it is a laboratory test.
StepWorkingResult
1Questionnaire sensitivity = 200 / 25080%
2Questionnaire specificity = 120 / 15080%
3Assay sensitivity = 175 / 25070%
4Assay specificity = 135 / 15090%
5Assay versus questionnaireSensitivity down 10 points, specificity up 10 points
Column by column: the urine assay catches 70% of the 250 dependent attenders (lower) and clears 90% of the 150 non-dependent (higher).

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308: 1552.

A new self-report questionnaire for adult ADHD is tried on 150 adults with a confirmed diagnosis and 250 adults known not to have ADHD. It is positive in 120 of the cases and in 50 of the controls, as the table shows. The specificity and the false positive rate of the questionnaire are, respectively,
  1. 80% and 80%
  2. 80% and 20%
  3. 75% and 25%
  4. 20% and 80%
  5. 80% and 33%
Show the working
Answer: B 80% and 20%

Specificity is the share of non-diseased people the test correctly calls negative. Its complement, the false positive rate, is the share of non-diseased people wrongly called positive. The two must add to 100% because they describe the same column.

Of the 250 controls, 50 were positive (false positives) and 200 were negative (true negatives). Specificity = 200/250 = 80%; false positive rate = 50/250 = 20%. The 150 cases are irrelevant to either figure; they give sensitivity = 120/150 = 80%.

The exam gives sensitivity the same value as specificity here precisely so that a careless reading cannot be distinguished from a correct one until you check the second figure.

Rule: False positive rate = 1 minus specificity, always read from the non-diseased column.
Trap: Dividing the 50 false positives by the number of cases instead of the number of controls.
Among the 250 controls, 200 screen negative and 50 screen positive: specificity 200/250 = 80% and false positive rate 50/250 = 20%, adding to 100% because they share one column.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308: 1552.

Thirty patients had an aggressive incident and 30 did not. The checklist was positive in 24 of those who went on to have an incident, and negative in 27 of those who did not. What is the overall accuracy of the checklist?

  2. 51/60
  3. 27/30
  4. 24/60

Answer: B 51/60

Accuracy is the proportion of all classifications that were right. It takes the two 'correct' diagonal cells of the 2x2 table and divides by the grand total.

True positives 24, true negatives 27, total 60. Accuracy = 51/60 = 0.85. The remaining 9 (3 false positives and 6 false negatives) are the errors.

The exam sometimes phrases this as 'the proportion correctly classified'. It is a weak summary because it ignores which kind of error dominates, but it is a frequent one-mark question.

Rule: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / everyone tested.
Trap: Using only one correct cell (24/60) or only one column.

Sensitivity conditions on the outcome: among those who truly have it, what share does the test flag? It is a column calculation using true positives and false negatives.

Thirty patients had an incident; the checklist flagged 24 of them. Sensitivity = 24/30 = 0.80. The 6 missed are the false negatives.

The wording 'probability of a positive test in someone with the condition' is the exam's standard definition of sensitivity; the mirror phrase 'probability of the condition in someone with a positive test' is PPV. Read the direction of the conditional.

Rule: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN), read down the outcome-present column.
Trap: Reading 'positive' and 'incident' in the wrong order and answering the PPV.

A four-item nursing risk checklist on admission against aggressive incidents recorded in the first week, 60 acute ward admissions
A four-item nursing risk checklist is completed on admission for 60 consecutive acute ward admissions, and incident records over the following week are used as the reference standard. Thirty patients had an aggressive incident and 30 did not. The checklist was positive in 24 of those who went on to have an incident, and negative in 27 of those who did not. How many times more likely is a positive checklist in a patient who goes on to have an aggressive incident than in one who does not?
  1. 0.8
  2. 2
  3. 8
  4. 12
  5. 24
Show the working
Answer: C 8

The positive likelihood ratio compares how often a positive result occurs in those with the outcome against how often it occurs in those without. It is sensitivity divided by the false positive rate.

Sensitivity = 24/30 = 0.80. False positive rate = 3/30 = 0.10. LR+ = 0.80 / 0.10 = 8. A positive checklist is eight times as likely in a patient who will have an incident as in one who will not.

The exam words this as 'how many times more likely is a positive result in the diseased'. That phrase is the definition of LR+; do not confuse it with the odds ratio from the same table, which would be (24 x 27) / (3 x 6) = 36.

Rule: LR+ = true positive rate / false positive rate.
Trap: Computing the odds ratio of the 2x2 table instead of the likelihood ratio.
A positive checklist appears in 24 of 30 (80%) who go on to an incident but in only 3 of 30 (10%) who do not: 0.80 / 0.10 = 8, the positive likelihood ratio.

Source: Deeks JJ, Altman DG (2004). Diagnostic tests 4: likelihood ratios. BMJ, 329: 168-169.

The table shows the performance of a 12-item postnatal distress questionnaire in detecting psychiatric disorder six weeks after a stillbirth, at several cut-offs. If a score above 3 is taken as positive, which of the following is true?
  1. Everyone without a disorder will be correctly excluded
  2. A positive result means the woman is certain to have a disorder
  3. Everyone with a disorder will be correctly identified
  4. Few women without a disorder will be wrongly labelled
  5. A negative result still leaves a substantial chance of disorder
Show the working
Answer: C Everyone with a disorder will be correctly identified

Each cell of the table maps to a statement about errors. Sensitivity of 100% means the false negative count is zero: nobody with the disorder is missed. Specificity of 100% would mean zero false positives. PPV of 100% would mean every positive is a true case.

At the lowest cut-off (above 3) sensitivity is 100% and NPV is 100%, both of which say the same thing: no one with the disorder slipped through. But specificity is only 62% and PPV 18%, so most positives are false alarms and many well women are flagged.

The exam turns percentages into sentences. Translate each option back into which cell would have to be zero or full, then check the table.

Rule: Sensitivity 100% = no false negatives; specificity 100% = no false positives.
Trap: Reading NPV 100% as 'everyone without the disorder is excluded', which would be specificity.
StatementWhich figure must holdAt cut-off >3
Everyone with a disorder identifiedSensitivity = 100% (false negatives = 0)True at >3 (the answer)
Everyone without a disorder excludedSpecificity = 100% (false positives = 0)False: specificity 62%
A positive means certain disorderPPV = 100%False: PPV 18%
Few well women wrongly labelledSpecificity highFalse: 38% of well women flagged
A negative still leaves a real chance of disorderNPV well below 100%False: NPV 100%
Each statement is a claim about one cell of the table; at a cut-off above 3 only the sensitivity claim holds, because sensitivity 100% means no false negatives.

The table shows scores on a four-item gambling screen against a structured diagnostic interview in 120 attenders at a debt advice service. If answering yes to at least three of the four items is taken as a positive screen, what is the sensitivity of the screen?
  1. 20%
  2. 30%
  3. 50%
  4. 80%
  5. 100%
Show the working
Answer: C 50%

A score table is not yet a 2x2 table. A cut-off of 3 means everyone scoring 3 or 4 is test positive and everyone scoring 0, 1 or 2 is test negative. You collapse the rows into those two groups before calculating anything.

Disorder present column: scores 3 and 4 give 12 + 8 = 20 test positives, and scores 0 to 2 give 2 + 6 + 12 = 20 test negatives. Sensitivity = 20/40 = 50%. For completeness, specificity at this cut-off is (44 + 24 + 12)/80 = 80/80 = 100%, since no unaffected person scored 3 or more.

The exam's trap is to read a single row rather than accumulating. Always ask 'which rows are positive at this cut-off' and add them.

Rule: At a cut-off, 'positive' means that score and every score above it; add the rows cumulatively.
Trap: Using only the row for a score of exactly 3 rather than 3 and above.
At a cut-off of 3 or more, 20 of the 40 people with the disorder screen positive (sensitivity 50%) and none of the 80 without it do (specificity 100%).

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.

Receiver operating characteristic curve of a seven-item self-rated anxiety scale against a structured interview in 310 primary care attenders, with the diagonal reference line; numbered cut-offs
A seven-item self-rated anxiety scale was evaluated against a structured diagnostic interview in 310 primary care attenders, and the figure was plotted from the data. The horizontal axis is labelled 1 minus specificity. What does this quantity represent?
  1. True negative rate
  2. False negative rate
  3. True positive rate
  4. False positive rate
  5. Accuracy
Show the working
Answer: D False positive rate

Within the non-diseased column, everyone is either a true negative or a false positive, so the two proportions add to 1. Specificity is the true negative share; 1 minus specificity is therefore the false positive share.

A ROC curve plots the benefit of a test (true positive rate, sensitivity) against its cost (false positive rate, 1 minus specificity). That is why the ideal corner is top left: all benefit, no cost.

The exam asks the same thing for 1 minus sensitivity, which is the false negative rate. Keep the pair straight: 'minus sensitivity' lives in the diseased column, 'minus specificity' in the non-diseased column.

Rule: 1 minus specificity = false positive rate.
Trap: Answering false negative rate by swapping sensitivity and specificity.
Where it livesNamed quantityIts complement
Non-diseased columnSpecificity = true negative rate1 minus specificity = false positive rate (the answer)
Diseased columnSensitivity = true positive rate1 minus sensitivity = false negative rate
ROC axesVertical: sensitivity (benefit)Horizontal: 1 minus specificity (cost)
Each column adds to 1: the complement of specificity is the false positive share of the non-diseased, which is the ROC horizontal axis.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 3: receiver operating characteristic plots. BMJ, 309: 188.

Distribution of questionnaire scores in patients with and without a depressive disorder, with four candidate cut-offs (a score at or above the cut-off is a positive screen)
The figure shows the distribution of scores on a 9-item mood questionnaire in primary care attenders with and without a depressive disorder, with four candidate cut-offs A (8), B (10), C (12) and D (14). A score at or above the cut-off counts as a positive screen. Which cut-off gives the highest sensitivity?
  1. A
  2. B
  3. C
  4. D
  5. Sensitivity is the same at all four
Show the working
Answer: A A

In an overlap figure the two curves show how scores are distributed in people with and without the condition. A cut-off slices both. The area of the affected curve on the positive side is the sensitivity; the area of the unaffected curve on the negative side is the specificity. Sliding the cut-off towards the unaffected curve captures more cases (higher sensitivity) but also more non-cases (lower specificity).

Cut-off A at a score of 8 sits about 1.75 SDs below the depressed mean of 15 (SD 4), so roughly 96% of cases score at or above it. At D (14) the cut-off is just below the depressed mean, so only about 60% of cases are captured. Sensitivity therefore runs A > B > C > D.

The exam sets this up with the direction of positivity stated in the stem. If a lower score were positive (as with a cognitive test) the ordering would reverse. Read the axis direction before you answer.

Rule: When higher scores are positive, the lowest cut-off gives the highest sensitivity (and the lowest specificity).
Trap: Reversing the direction because the labels are read left to right without checking which side is positive.
StepWorkingResult
A (8)z = (8 minus 15)/4 = -1.75about 96% of cases at or above
B (10)z = (10 minus 15)/4 = -1.25about 89%
C (12)z = (12 minus 15)/4 = -0.75about 77%
D (14)z = (14 minus 15)/4 = -0.25about 60%
OrderSensitivity A > B > C > DA is highest: the answer
Sensitivity is the share of the depressed curve (mean 15, SD 4) at or above each cut-off: 96%, 89%, 77%, 60%.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308: 1552.

Distribution of questionnaire scores in patients with and without a depressive disorder, with four candidate cut-offs (a score at or above the cut-off is a positive screen)
The figure shows the distribution of scores on a 9-item mood questionnaire in primary care attenders with and without a depressive disorder, with four candidate cut-offs A (8), B (10), C (12) and D (14). A score at or above the cut-off counts as a positive screen. The practice wants to minimise the number of patients without a depressive disorder who are referred unnecessarily. Which cut-off should it choose?
  1. A
  2. B
  3. C
  4. D
  5. Any cut-off gives the same number of unnecessary referrals
Show the working
Answer: D D

Unnecessary referrals are false positives: people without the condition who screen positive. Their number is governed by specificity (and prevalence). On the overlap figure the false positive fraction is the part of the unaffected curve lying on the positive side of the cut-off. The further the cut-off is pushed into the affected curve, the smaller that tail becomes.

The healthy curve has mean 6 and SD 3. The tail at or above each cut-off is roughly: A (8) about 25%, B (10) about 9%, C (12) about 2%, D (14) under 1%. D produces the fewest false positives, at the cost of a sensitivity of only about 60%, so the practice must be clear that it is prioritising specificity over not missing cases.

The exam phrases the goal in service terms ('avoid overloading the service', 'reduce unnecessary referrals', 'confirm before treating'); all mean maximise specificity. The mirror question ('avoid missing anyone') means maximise sensitivity.

Rule: To cut false positives, choose the most specific cut-off, the one furthest from the unaffected curve.
Trap: Choosing the balanced cut-off (C) when the question asks only about false positives.
StepWorkingResult
A (8)z = (8 minus 6)/3 = 0.67about 25% of non-cases positive
B (10)z = 1.33about 9%
C (12)z = 2.00about 2.3%
D (14)z = 2.67about 0.4%: fewest, the answer
CostSensitivity at Donly about 60%
False positives are the healthy curve's tail (mean 6, SD 3) above each cut-off; D leaves under 1%.

Source: Altman DG, Bland JM (1994). Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity. BMJ, 308: 1552.

The positive predictive value answers the clinical question 'this woman has screened positive; how likely is she to have the disorder?'. It is calculated along the test-positive row and depends heavily on prevalence: the rarer the condition, the more of the positive screens are false alarms.

Here 270 women screened positive, of whom 90 truly have an anxiety disorder. PPV = 90/270 = 0.33. Despite a sensitivity of 0.90, two in three positive screens are false positives, because the prevalence is only 10% and the 180 false positives outnumber the 90 true ones.

The exam likes the contrast: high sensitivity, modest PPV. When the stem gives you a low-prevalence screening setting, expect the PPV to be unimpressive and check that your answer reflects it.

In a diagnostic accuracy study it is the column total for the condition divided by the grand total of everyone assessed with the reference standard. Here there are 50 attenders with gambling disorder and 450 without, 500 in all. Prevalence = 50/500 = 0.10, or 10%. Dividing cases by non-cases instead (50/450 = 0.11) gives the odds, which is the usual slip and is why 11% appears as an option.

Answer: C 20%

Pre-test probability is the chance that a particular person has the condition before the test result is known. In a screening setting, where nothing else distinguishes the individual, the natural estimate is the prevalence in that population. It is the left-hand axis of the nomogram.

The clinic prevalence is 20%, so an attender walks in with a 20% probability of depression. The sensitivity and specificity belong to the questionnaire and are used to form the likelihood ratio in the next step; they are not probabilities for the patient.

The exam places sensitivity, likelihood ratio and post-test probability among the options to see whether you reach for the only number that describes the population: the prevalence.

Rule: Pre-test probability = prevalence in the population from which the patient comes.
Trap: Picking the sensitivity because it is the first test property quoted.
TermFormula or meaningThis item
Pre-test probabilityChance of the condition before the test; in screening, the prevalence20%: the left axis of the nomogram
Sensitivity 80%, specificity 90%Properties of the questionnaireCombine into LR+ = 0.80/0.10 = 8, the middle axis
Post-test probabilityWhere the line lands on the right axis67%, used in the next question
Only the prevalence describes the attender before testing: pre-test probability = 20%; sensitivity and specificity belong to the questionnaire

Source: Fagan TJ (1975). Nomogram for Bayes theorem. NEJM, 293: 257.

Challenge 29 · 13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.7
Nomogram for a depression screening questionnaire used in a diabetes clinic: pre-test probability 20%, positive likelihood ratio 8
A depression screening questionnaire is used in a diabetes outpatient clinic. Previous work has established that 20% of attenders at this clinic have a depressive disorder. The questionnaire has a sensitivity of 80% and a specificity of 90%. The nomogram is provided. Using the nomogram, what is the probability that an attender who screens positive truly has a depressive disorder?
  1. 20%
  2. 35%
  3. 50%
  4. 67%
  5. 85%
Show the working
Answer: D 67%

The nomogram is a graphical Bayes theorem. A straight line from the pre-test probability on the left, through the likelihood ratio in the middle, meets the post-test probability on the right. Underneath, the arithmetic is: convert the pre-test probability to odds, multiply by the likelihood ratio, convert the post-test odds back to a probability.

Pre-test probability 20% is odds of 0.20/0.80 = 0.25. Multiply by LR+ 8 to get post-test odds of 2 (that is 2:1). Probability = 2/(1 + 2) = 0.667, about 67%. Drawing the line on the nomogram from 20% through 8 lands on roughly the same figure. Note that this is the positive predictive value in this clinic.

The exam gives several options spaced along the right-hand axis. If you cannot read the figure precisely, do the odds arithmetic and choose the option nearest to it; the keyed answer always sits well away from its neighbours.

Rule: Post-test odds = pre-test odds x LR; convert back with probability = odds / (1 + odds).
Trap: Multiplying the pre-test probability (not the odds) by the LR, which gives 160% and nonsense.
24 attenders screen positive and 16 of them are truly depressed: 16/24 = 67%, the same figure the nomogram line gives

Source: Fagan TJ (1975). Nomogram for Bayes theorem. NEJM, 293: 257.

Challenge 30 · 13.2 Diagnostic accuracy · 3.2.7
Pre-test probability 10% and LR+ of 6
A 72-year-old man scores below the cut-off (a positive screen for dementia) on a six-item cognitive screen that has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 85% for dementia. The prevalence of dementia in men of his age in the practice is 10%. What is the probability that he actually has dementia?
  1. 0.10
  2. 0.40
  3. 0.60
  4. 0.85
  5. 0.90
Show the working
Answer: B 0.40

A likelihood ratio moves you from what you believed before the test to what you should believe after it, but it works on odds, not probabilities. Convert prevalence to odds, multiply by the likelihood ratio for the result obtained, then convert back.

LR+ = sensitivity / (1 minus specificity) = 0.90 / 0.15 = 6. Prevalence 10% is pre-test odds of 1 to 9. Post-test odds = 6 x 1/9 = 0.667. Probability = 0.667 / 1.667 = 0.40. The Fagan nomogram in the figure gives the same reading.

The exam will offer sensitivity, specificity and the prevalence as distractors. Any answer equal to one of the given numbers is almost never the post-test probability.

Rule: Post-test odds = pre-test odds x LR; convert odds to probability with odds / (1 + odds).
Trap: Multiplying the LR by the prevalence directly (6 x 0.10 = 0.60) instead of by the odds.
Of 200 men, 20 have dementia and the screen catches 18; of the 180 without, 15% (27) also screen positive; so among the 45 positives only 18 are real: 18/45 = 0.40.

Source: Deeks JJ, Altman DG (2004). Diagnostic tests 4: likelihood ratios. BMJ, 329: 168-169.
